title: Big Oil asks Supreme Court to kill climate lawsuits before trial
gist: The US Supreme Court heard ExxonMobil and Suncor's bid to have federal law preempt Boulder's climate-deception lawsuit, a case that could decide the fate of more than two dozen similar suits; justices questioned whether it was too early to intervene, and Alito's recusal opens the possibility of a tie that would let the case proceed.

insights.claim: More than two dozen state and local lawsuits accuse oil companies of deceiving the public about climate change and seek potentially billions in damages; many are paused pending the Supreme Court's ruling in Boulder's case, expected by June.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: A single ruling will either end or unleash multi-billion-dollar liability exposure for oil majors.
insights.quote: The decision, expected by the end of the court’s term in June, could bring those claims to an abrupt halt or set the stage for trials to finally begin.
insights.locator: Many of the cases brought by states

insights.claim: Exxon and Suncor's counsel argued that allowing Boulder's claims would let some 90,000 municipalities make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected producers.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Industry frames the risk as open-ended, fragmented liability — the core reason it seeks a preemption ruling now.
insights.quote: some 90,000 municipalities across the country would have the ability to make national and international energy policy

insights.claim: Boulder counters that its case seeks damages for deception rather than any limit on emissions, likening it to state actions like gas taxes that only secondarily reduce pollution.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Framing as deception rather than emissions regulation is plaintiffs' path around Clean Air Act preemption.
insights.quote: This case is not about emissions,” said Kevin Russell, who argued the case for Boulder. “It’s about deception.”
insights.locator: This case is not about emissions

insights.claim: Columbia's Michael Gerrard views Boulder's best shot as the jurisdictional question of whether the case is too early, as several justices suggested premature intervention.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
entities: Sabin Center for Climate Change Law
insights.so_what: A jurisdictional dismissal would leave the merits unresolved and let suits proceed toward trial.
insights.quote: I think Boulder’s best shot is on the jurisdictional question, whether this case is too early,

insights.claim: Several conservative justices appeared inclined to agree that federal law preempts at least some of Boulder's claims, according to Gerrard.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: On the merits, odds lean toward at least partial preemption favorable to oil companies.
insights.quote: Several of the conservative justices seemed inclined to agree that federal law preempts at least some of Boulder’s claims

insights.claim: Justice Alito recused himself, reportedly under pressure over his stock holdings in oil companies party to related suits, creating the possibility of a tie vote that would let the case proceed.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: An eight-justice bench materially raises the chance plaintiffs survive this round.
insights.quote: Alito’s absence leaves open the possibility of a tie vote, which would allow the case to move forward.

insights.claim: Oil companies and conservative groups are ramping up efforts to block the suits: some states have enacted bars, Republicans introduced federal liability-shield legislation, and the Trump administration intervened in several cases including Boulder's.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Legislative liability shields are a parallel path that could moot litigation regardless of the court outcome.
insights.quote: Republicans have introduced federal legislation that would shield oil companies from climate liability claims.

insights.claim: Scientists whose work is cited in the cases have been targeted with more than 100 public records requests from conservative groups seeking information on their work and funders, according to Politico.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Pressure on the evidentiary base is part of the defense strategy.
insights.quote: have been the subject of more than 100 public records requests from conservative groups

insights.claim: Boulder drew supportive briefs not only from climate groups and Democrats but also from former EPA officials including some appointed by Republican presidents.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Bipartisan expert support weakens the framing of the suits as purely partisan.
insights.quote: former Environmental Protection Agency officials, including some appointed by Republican presidents.
